title: India Just Hiked Gold Duties to 15 Per Cent and HDFC Suspended Subscriptions. Here Is What NRIs Should Do.
excerpt: Domestic prices surged, ETF inflows hit a wall, and global gold is trapped between war premiums and rate hike fears. A complete guide for diaspora investors.
body:
India just made gold significantly more expensive to buy, and one of the country's largest fund houses has started turning investors away. If you hold gold in any form — jewellery, coins, ETFs, sovereign gold bonds, or digital gold — the rules of the game changed this month.

Here is what happened, why it matters, and what NRI investors should be thinking about right now.

## The Duty Shock

On May 13, India raised import duties on gold and silver from 6 per cent to 15 per cent. The stated goal: curb overseas purchases, ease pressure on foreign exchange reserves that have been strained by elevated oil prices from the Iran conflict, and narrow a widening trade deficit.

The impact was immediate. Domestic gold prices surged to 164,497 rupees per 10 grams, their highest level in more than two months. As of this week, gold is trading at around 158,400 rupees per 10 grams — still significantly above pre-duty levels.

India is the world's second-largest gold consumer after China. The duty hike is designed to hurt. And it is working: dealers are now quoting discounts of up to $87 per ounce over official domestic prices, down from $106 the previous week but still deep enough to signal that demand is cooling.

## HDFC Mutual Fund Pulls the Shutters

On Thursday, HDFC Mutual Fund — one of India's largest asset managers — announced it would suspend lump-sum subscriptions of 250 million rupees ($2.61 million) and above in its Gold ETF from June 8. It also capped new investments in its Gold ETF Fund of Fund at 1 million rupees per investor per month, effective June 5.

The reason: large investments are difficult for gold ETFs to absorb during periods of heavy demand. Despite May's net outflow of $61 million (the first monthly outflow in a year), gold ETFs have attracted net inflows of $3.48 billion so far in 2026. Total holdings stand at 116.3 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council.

This is not a one-off. When India's largest fund house starts capping subscriptions, it signals that the domestic gold market is under structural pressure from both regulatory tightening and overwhelming investor demand.

## The Global Picture Is Complicated

Gold hit a record high of $5,594.82 per ounce in January 2026. Since then, it has lost about 16 per cent of its value, and the reasons are counterintuitive.

The Iran conflict should, in theory, drive gold higher. It is the textbook safe-haven trade. Instead, the war has pushed oil prices to nearly $93 per barrel, which has stoked inflation fears, which has raised expectations of interest rate hikes, which suppresses non-yielding assets like gold.

On Friday, gold fell 3.3 per cent to around $4,328 per ounce after the US jobs report showed 172,000 new jobs in May — roughly double what economists expected. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped past 4.5 per cent. Traders now see a 43 per cent chance the Federal Reserve hikes rates by December, up from 26 per cent a month ago.

Germany's Commerzbank cut its year-end gold target from $5,000 to $4,800 this week, its first downward revision of 2026. The bank's analyst Daniel Fritsch tied the cut explicitly to the oil-driven rate shock, not to any change in gold's structural bull case.

Central banks bought 243.7 metric tonnes in Q1 2026, up 3 per cent year-on-year. But the pace is levelling off. Global jewellery demand dropped 25 per cent to 260.2 tonnes. India's jewellery demand slipped 19 per cent to 66.1 tonnes.

## What NRIs Should Consider

**If you are buying gold for a wedding or festival in India**: The 15 per cent duty has made it substantially more expensive to buy domestically. Some NRIs are instead purchasing gold abroad and carrying it in (India allows up to a certain weight under personal allowance), but this has its own duty implications and is subject to customs scrutiny. Check the latest personal carriage limits before you travel.

**If you hold Indian gold ETFs**: HDFC's subscription caps do not affect existing holdings, but they signal that large allocations may face friction going forward. If you are building a position, consider spreading purchases over several months rather than making a lump-sum commitment.

**If you hold US-listed gold ETFs (GLD, IAU)**: These are unaffected by India's duty changes. They track global gold prices, which are currently being pushed around more by oil and interest rate expectations than by traditional safe-haven demand. A ceasefire in the Iran conflict could be the catalyst that lifts gold back toward $5,000, as falling oil would reduce rate hike fears.

**If you are considering gold as a portfolio hedge**: The traditional inverse correlation between gold and equities is not working cleanly right now. On Friday, stocks fell and gold fell too. In this environment, gold is behaving more like a rate-sensitive asset than a crisis hedge. That does not mean it is a bad holding — central bank buying provides a structural floor — but do not assume it will protect you in a selloff.

The wedding season in India is drawing to a close, which typically reduces seasonal demand. The next major demand pulse will come during Dhanteras and Diwali later this year. By then, the market should have more clarity on Iran, oil, and the Fed's next move.

Until then, the message from India's regulators is clear: they want you to buy less gold, and they are using every tool available to make that happen.
